name: Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids: tobacco-control and health policy campaigns (charityevals, 2024-25)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults. Tobacco wins in the ten priority countries (72%), split by their smoking DALYs (GBD 2023); US tobacco wins (9%); the Global Health Advocacy Incubator's food, injury and health-system wins in 38 countries (18%), spread by world population.
summary: The Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids campaigns for tobacco-control laws: in ten low- and middle-income priority countries and Africa ($29.5m in the year to March 2025, much of it paid for by Bloomberg Philanthropies' restricted grants), in the US ($8.4m: taxes, flavour rules, FDA regulation) and, through its Global Health Advocacy Incubator ($6.1m), on food, road safety and other health policy. Each branch is CTFK's share of the people and money behind a typical recent year's wins (12% in the US, 15% abroad) times the share of the smoking or diet burden those wins avert (0.25% a year of the priority countries' smoking burden), anchored on estimates of what the world's tobacco-control policies of 2007–2020 achieved; deaths are valued by age, half the cut in smoking pays off after about 8 years (quitters) and half after about 30 (young people who never start), and second-hand smoke is counted as a side effect. The result, about 0.13 years of healthy life per $1,000, is above the median of the site's global-health models because tobacco kills about 1.6 million people a year in the priority countries and a won tax or law lasts, but it is dominated by judgment (the share of the burden a year's wins avert and CTFK's credit for them), all three branches are discounted for missing data, since no change in smoking from CTFK's own wins is measured, and the next dollar counts at 42% of the average.

rows.label: US: share of US smoking DALYs a typical year's US tobacco-control wins avert once in full effect
rows.explainer: A year's US wins by all groups: one or two state tax rises (Indiana's $2 a pack in 2025), local flavour bans (Denver's, upheld by voters in November 2024), Tobacco 21 and e-cigarette enforcement and court wins (FDA v. Wages and White Lion, April 2025), against setbacks (the FDA's menthol ban withdrawn in January 2025). Worked out as in charityevals' American Cancer Society model: a $1 rise on an $8 pack cuts cigarette consumption about 5% (price elasticity about -0.4), and the number of smokers about half as much, 2.5% (about half the response is quitting, half smoking less); one or two states' rises cover a few percent of Americans, about 0.1% fewer smokers nationally; flavour and youth rules (fewer young people starting) about 1.5 times as much again. 0.25%, 0.08% to 0.7%. Long-run fall in smoking, so it reads as a share of the smoking burden in the steady state.

rows.label: Global: share of the ten countries' smoking DALYs a typical year's wins there avert once in full effect
rows.explainer: Reference class: Lyle and Hendrie (Globalization and Health, 2024) estimate that the MPOWER policies 136 countries adopted at the highest level in 2007–2020 cut smokers by 81.0 million (about 7% of the world's smokers over 14 years, 0.5% a year), but by only 8.57 million in 2016–2020 (about 0.16% a year); in that latest period their only entries for the ten countries are the Philippines (cessation, 519,000 fewer smokers), Pakistan (warnings, 1.62 million) and Brazil (tax, none): about 0.14% a year of the ten countries' smokers. The 2020–2025 wins are more: Pakistan's 2023 tax rise (cigarette excise up about 150%), Mexico's 2023 smoke-free and total advertising ban, Indonesia's 2024 regulation (minimum age 21, single-stick and advertising limits), yearly tax rises in the Philippines, Bangladesh and Ukraine, and the 2024 e-cigarette bans in Vietnam and Mexico (counted here as nothing for smoking). 0.25% a year, 0.1% to 0.8%: the long-run cut in smokers reads as a share of the burden in the steady state. Not built bottom up from each win's effect size (a judgment on the period's rate).

rows.label: GHAI: share of the world's obesity and salt DALYs a typical year's food-policy wins avert once in full effect
rows.explainer: GHAI reports 217 policies passed or strengthened in 38 countries (its home page, no start year); spread over the ten or so years it has run inside CTFK (a judgment), about 20 a year across all its areas; food policies are front-of-pack warning labels (Chile's cut sugary-drink purchases about 24% in the first year), sugary-drink taxes (about 10% fewer purchases per 10% price), trans-fat limits and salt targets, each in a country with a few percent of the world's burden. A typical year: about two food wins in countries with about 4% of the world's burden, each cutting it about 0.5% in the long run, so 0.02%; 0.003% to 0.1%.

rows.label: GHAI: burden its other areas' wins avert, as a share of its food wins'
rows.explainer: Road safety (speed and helmet laws), drowning prevention, overdose prevention, immunization and health-data budgets: about half of GHAI's work by its programme list. Judged at 50% of the food wins' DALYs, 20% to 100%; the deaths are valued as diet-related ones (mostly older adults), which undervalues the younger road and drowning deaths a little.

rows.label: Tobacco: share of a policy's long-run cut in smoking that comes in its first years (smokers quitting)
rows.explainer: Lyle and Hendrie (2024, Methods) take the long-term effect, the change in prevalence after 40 years, as the first-year effect times a multiplier for each policy: 2 for taxes and warnings, 1.25 for smoke-free laws, 1.3 for marketing bans, 2.5 for cessation. So about half of the long-run cut (40% to 80%: one over the multipliers) comes at once, from smokers who quit; the rest builds over decades from young people who never start. 0.5, 0.35 to 0.75.

rows.label: Tobacco: years from quitting until the health gain
rows.explainer: Smokers who quit cut their heart-disease risk within a few years and their cancer and lung-disease risk over 5 to 20; the burden a quitter averts comes on average about 8 years later. 8 years, 3 to 15.

rows.label: Tobacco: years from a young person not starting until the health gain
rows.explainer: Young people kept from starting would have died of smoking mostly after 50, three to five decades later; the effect itself builds up over the 40 years of Lyle and Hendrie's long run. 30 years, 20 to 40.

rows.label: Tobacco: discount for the wait from the policy to the health gain
rows.explainer: The quitters' share at their lag and the never-starters' share at theirs, each discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: GHAI: years from the policy taking effect until the health gain
rows.explainer: Less salt lowers blood pressure within weeks and heart attacks and strokes within a few years; less sugary drink acts on weight over years; road and drowning laws act at once. 5 years, 1 to 15: shorter than tobacco's.

rows.label: Advocacy: share of the wins counted that this period's work produced
rows.explainer: 1: the branches count a typical year's wins already won against the same years' spending (a past average), and the chance that the work made a difference is the credit share (attribution) and the years a win counts ($win_years_counted).

rows.label: Advocacy: years a won reform counts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a won policy counts before it would have come anyway (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Advocacy: years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: Taxes take effect at once or at the next budget year; regulations and bans within months to two years (Indonesia's 2024 regulation phases in; Vietnam's e-cigarette ban took effect in January 2025). 1 year, 0.25 to 2.

rows.label: Advocacy: discounted years of impact
rows.explainer: The years a win counts and the wait until it takes effect, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: US: DALYs averted by a typical year's US wins (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: US smoking DALYs × the share averted × the health lag × the years counted.

rows.label: Global: DALYs averted by a typical year's wins in the priority countries (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The ten countries' smoking DALYs × the share averted × the health lag × the years counted.

rows.label: GHAI: DALYs averted by a typical year's wins (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Obesity and salt DALYs × the share averted × (1 + the other areas) × the health lag × the years counted.

rows.label: Expected DALYs averted by advocacy (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The three branches summed.

rows.explainer: Diet-related deaths are mostly heart disease and stroke: the shared world cardiovascular figure.

rows.label: GHAI: share of DALYs that are illness (cardiovascular, world)
rows.explainer: The shared world cardiovascular figure; kept as DALYs.

rows.label: US: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: Only the validity of the effect sizes (unmeasured outcomes are the missing-data discount, leakage the enforcement row): price elasticities and flavour-restriction studies are well established in the US; the step from fewer smokers to less burden in the steady state is less sure. 0.8, 0.5 to 1.

rows.label: US: counterfactual
rows.explainer: 1: whether the policy would have come anyway is the years a win counts ($win_years_counted), one question (Convention 5).

rows.label: US: CTFK's share of the people and money behind the wins
rows.explainer: US tobacco wins are coalition wins: ACS CAN (whose own model credits it 30% of its wins across all its issues), the American Heart Association, the American Lung Association, Truth Initiative, state and local health departments and coalitions, and CTFK's own 501(c)(4) Action Fund, which pays for most direct lobbying. CTFK is a lead strategist (state tax campaigns, FDA litigation, the yearly state reports). 12%, 5% to 25% of the people and money behind the wins.

rows.label: US: attribution share
rows.explainer: The share of resources (Convention 2).

rows.label: US: share of the wins enforced as written
rows.explainer: US taxes are collected and age and flavour rules mostly enforced; illegal disposable e-cigarettes and cross-border buying leak some of the effect. 0.9, 0.75 to 1.

rows.label: US: discount for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): no measured change in smoking or health from CTFK's own wins, only projections from the research on such policies.

rows.label: US: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: US: illness averted, credited (DALYs)
rows.explainer: The illness part of the branch's DALYs, kept as DALYs, after its adjustments and side effects.

rows.label: US: deaths averted, valued by age, credited (units of value)
rows.formula: us_dalys * (1 - us_yld_share) * us_deaths_per_daly * us_value_per_death * us_total_adj * (1 + us_side_effects)
rows.explainer: The deaths behind the rest of the branch's DALYs, valued by age, after its adjustments and side effects.

rows.label: Global: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: Only the validity of the effect sizes (unmeasured outcomes are the missing-data discount, illicit trade and laws on paper the enforcement row): SimSmoke's effect sizes come from high-income countries and are moved to LMICs with adjustors for awareness and urbanisation; Lyle and Hendrie's own bounds are about ±50% (1.68 to 5.05 million deaths averted on 3.37 million in 2016–2020). 0.8, 0.5 to 1.

rows.label: Global: counterfactual
rows.explainer: 1: whether the policy would have come anyway is the years a win counts ($win_years_counted), one question (Convention 5).

rows.label: Global: CTFK's share of the people and money behind the wins
rows.explainer: Behind the wins: ministries of health and finance (whose staff do the work), the other Bloomberg Initiative partners (Vital Strategies, The Union, Johns Hopkins, the University of Illinois Chicago, WHO), the Gates Foundation in Africa, and the local groups CTFK funds (its $9.6m of grants count as its own). Bloomberg Philanthropies gave about $60m a year to tobacco control in 2017–2022 ($360m over six years, Health Affairs 2017) and committed $420m over 2023–2026 (its February 2023 release); CTFK's $29.5m global programme is mostly Bloomberg money inside that total, not added to it. 15%, 7% to 30% of all resources, governments' included.

rows.label: Global: attribution share
rows.explainer: The share of resources (Convention 2).

rows.label: Global: share of the wins enforced as written
rows.explainer: Enforcement in LMICs is partial: smoke-free and advertising laws are weakly policed in many of these countries (WHO rates compliance), taxes leak to illicit and cheaper products. Lyle and Hendrie's effect sizes already carry compliance adjustors for smoke-free laws and marketing bans, so only the rest is counted here. 0.75, 0.5 to 0.9.

rows.label: Global: discount for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): no measured change in smoking or health from CTFK's own wins, only projections from the research on such policies.

rows.label: Global: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Global: illness averted, credited (DALYs)
rows.explainer: The illness part of the branch's DALYs, kept as DALYs, after its adjustments and side effects.

rows.label: Global: deaths averted, valued by age, credited (units of value)
rows.formula: glob_dalys * (1 - glob_yld_share) * glob_deaths_per_daly * glob_value_per_death * glob_total_adj * (1 + glob_side_effects)
rows.explainer: The deaths behind the rest of the branch's DALYs, valued by age, after its adjustments and side effects.

rows.label: GHAI: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: Food policies' effect on purchases is measured (Chile's labels, sugary-drink taxes); their effect on weight and disease is much less sure, and substitution to other foods offsets part. 0.5, 0.25 to 0.8.

rows.label: GHAI: counterfactual
rows.explainer: 1: whether the policy would have come anyway is the years a win counts ($win_years_counted), one question (Convention 5).

rows.label: GHAI: CTFK's share of the people and money behind the wins
rows.explainer: GHAI is an incubator: it funds and advises national coalitions, alongside governments, WHO, UNICEF and other funders (Bloomberg, Gates, Resolve to Save Lives). 15%, 5% to 30%.

rows.label: GHAI: attribution share
rows.explainer: The share of resources (Convention 2).

rows.label: GHAI: share of the wins enforced as written
rows.explainer: Labels, taxes and road laws are enforced in part; industry reformulation and court challenges delay some. 0.6, 0.35 to 0.85.

rows.label: GHAI: discount for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): no measured change in smoking or health from CTFK's own wins, only projections from the research on such policies.

rows.label: GHAI: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: GHAI: illness averted, credited (DALYs)
rows.explainer: The illness part of the branch's DALYs, kept as DALYs, after its adjustments and side effects.

rows.explainer: GBD 2023, the ten countries summed, for the global branch's second-hand-smoke side effect.

rows.label: US side effect: second-hand smoke burden averted, as a share of the smoking burden averted
rows.explainer: Fewer smokers means less second-hand smoke for the people around them, which GBD counts apart from smoking; smoke-free laws cut it directly. Taken as falling in step with smoking. Valued with the smokers' ages, though many second-hand-smoke deaths are children's (lower respiratory infections), which undervalues it. US: 1.0 million DALYs against 9.4 million for smoking (10%).

rows.label: Global side effect: second-hand smoke burden averted, as a share of the smoking burden averted
rows.explainer: Fewer smokers means less second-hand smoke for the people around them, which GBD counts apart from smoking; smoke-free laws cut it directly. Taken as falling in step with smoking. Valued with the smokers' ages, though many second-hand-smoke deaths are children's (lower respiratory infections), which undervalues it. Ten countries: 18.4 million DALYs against 47.8 million for smoking (38%).

rows.label: Global side effect: smokers kept from switching to e-cigarettes by the bans it backs, as a share of the value
rows.explainer: CTFK backs bans on e-cigarettes and heated tobacco in LMICs (Vietnam and Mexico in 2024, India in 2019, Brazil upheld in 2024). Where e-cigarettes help adults quit (Cochrane: higher quit rates than nicotine replacement), a ban keeps some smokers smoking; youth uptake averted runs the other way. Judged at -3% of the value, -15% to 0.

rows.label: Global side effect: money smokers' households no longer spend on tobacco, as a share of the value
rows.explainer: In poor households tobacco crowds out food and schooling (spending on tobacco is several percent of the budget in Bangladesh and Indonesia); quitting frees it, though taxes take part of it from those who keep smoking. Small next to the health gain: 3%, 0 to 10%.

rows.label: US: side effects, as a share of the branch's value
rows.explainer: Second-hand smoke, through the side-effects weight. E-cigarette rules in the US restrict flavours rather than ban, and households are richer: no other side effect counted.

rows.label: Global: side effects, as a share of the branch's value
rows.explainer: Second-hand smoke, e-cigarette bans and household spending, each through the side-effects weight.

rows.label: GHAI: side effects, as a share of the branch's value
rows.explainer: 0: no side effect of food, road or health-system policy is estimated; the tobacco side effects don't apply.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not in the branches, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: 0: the side effects are counted inside each branch (us_side_effects, glob_side_effects). Not counted: tax revenue (a transfer), industry litigation costs.
